source.title: Loss Spike in Training Neural Networks
source.authors: Xiaolong Li; Z. Xu; Zhongwang Zhang

record.file_problem: Text includes the full paper and appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally examines the relationship between Hessian maximum eigenvalue and generalization, and argues that this sharpness measure does not directly characterize generalization. It does not test any listed version’s specific measure or intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own eigendirection experiment on test loss. Learning-rate and condensation results do not measure the train–test generalization gap. Results from cited prior work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study examines loss spikes and unscaled Hessian eigendirections, not any listed claim version. Its test-loss intervention does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or rank generalization gaps as V7 requires. The batch-size comparison reports parameter projections without held-out performance or a fixed epoch comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors argue that the maximum Hessian eigenvalue characterizes sharpness relevant to linear stability but cannot directly characterize generalization, which involves many eigendirections, including small-eigenvalue directions. They also observe loss spikes facilitating condensation and propose a possible connection to generalization rather than demonstrating that connection.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines Hessian eigendirections and test loss, rather than magnitude-aware weight perturbations or a ranking of train–test gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: The tested tasks and network structures vary across figures; the paper reports differing eigendirection analyses for function fitting and CIFAR-10 classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing parameter components toward a test-fitted solution changes test loss little in leading Hessian eigendirections but substantially in smaller-eigenvalue directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The largest unscaled Hessian eigenvalue alone may fail to characterize generalization; directions with small eigenvalues can matter substantially.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Computational Mathematics (stated in supplied metadata; paper text labels itself a preprint).
record.problems: The eigendirection test-loss result is reported qualitatively in text, with precise values only in a figure. The comparison constructs θtest by further training θtrain on the test dataset, so it is not a standard held-out evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 6(d) compares parameter differences between small- and large-batch solutions by eigendirection but reports no held-out performance outcome. Figures 8–15 report loss spikes, λmax, or condensation, not generalization outcomes. Cited prior-work generalization results are excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting compared with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The criticism of maximum-eigenvalue sharpness does not establish a failure of V7's distinct magnitude-aware measure. Figure 6's parameter projections likewise do not measure V5's batch-size performance penalty.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and test error.
Large-batch versus small-batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: Two-layer tanh FNN with a width of 500
rows.operation_detail: Adjusted parameter differences along Hessian eigendirections and measured test loss as the number of adjusted directions increased.
rows.measure: Test loss change as differences between θtrain and θtest are eliminated in leading Hessian eigendirections.
rows.value: Movement on eigenvectors corresponding to large eigenvalues has weak impact on test loss; movement on eigenvectors corresponding to small eigenvalues has significant impact.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the effect; precise values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: The qualitative finding is correctly extracted, but cannot determine any listed version's effect. The baseline is test loss at θtrain, before replacing any eigendirection components, rather than unspecified. θtest is obtained by further training on the test data, so the intervention uses test labels and is not an independent held-out evaluation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
